2611.21758.abstract: We present NEMESIS II, a blind transit search of nearby M-dwarfs in TESS Primary Mission full-frame images (Sectors 1-26), including stars lacking 2-minute observations. Using the open-source NEMESIS pipeline, we extracted, detrended, and searched 213,658 single-sector light curves of 113,047 M-dwarfs within 100 pc, yielding 23,339 threshold crossing events. Automated LEO-Vetter vetting, applied identically to the survey and its injection-recovery and orbit-scrambling controls, retains 558 detections corresponding to 525 distinct signals with converged transit fits and periods of 0.51-9.10 days. Of these, 482 lie on stars without TOI, CTOI, or NASA Exoplanet Archive transiting-planet entries. Orbit-scrambling predicts 329 false alarms among the 558 detections, all but 14 of them among the 408 below Multiple Event Statistic 8. Assuming an astrophysical signal, TRICERATOPS favors a planetary origin for 262 of 525 candidates (232 new), which we classify as planet candidates; it also excludes resolved-neighbor eclipses for 105. Known planets and TOI candidates survive vetting at 1.01 +/- 0.07 of the injection-predicted rate. Correcting for each light curve's sensitivity, false alarms, and astrophysical false positives, we infer 0.81 +/- 0.44 planets per star for periods between 1.0-10.0 days and planet radii between 0.5-11.0 Earth radii. This is a lower limit, because our injections recover few or no planets near and below 1 Earth radii and assume central transits. Light curves, catalogs, vetting reports, and injection-recovery results will be released as a High Level Science Product at MAST upon publication. Documentation for the NEMESIS pipeline is available at this https URL.

2611.21841.abstract: Jupiter's circumpolar cyclones (CPCs) represent one of the most extreme dynamical regimes of the Solar System, where rotation, stratification, and convection interact to organize a stable polygonal cyclone lattice at each pole. Yet the depth and vertical structure of these cyclones remain unresolved. Here, using Juno Microwave Radiometer observations acquired between May 2023 and May 2024, we retrieve the 3-D thermal/compositional structure of Jupiter's northern CPCs at depths beyond those detectable by Earth-based telescopes and spacecraft that have ever visited. The eight CPCs, appearing with enhanced microwave brightness, show as modest ammonia depletion near the water lifting-condensation level ($\sim$5 bar) and/or, equivalently, warm-core structures analogous to terrestrial tropical cyclones. Five of them show substantially stronger and deeper anomalies than the remaining three, with approximately twice the inferred ammonia depletion and localized heating. In contrast, the central polar cyclone exhibits little microwave brightness contrast relative to its surroundings, despite its substantially cloudier and visually distinct appearance in visible and infrared observations. Previous dynamical models have treated the CPCs and the central polar cyclone as dynamically similar structures arising from the self-organization of turbulent flows. The new observations, however, suggest that the CPCs and the central polar cyclone may have distinct origins and operate under different dynamical regimes.

2611.21884.abstract: We present a Submillimeter Array (SMA) 1.3mm (225GHz) continuum emission survey of Young Stellar Objects (YSOs) in the Taurus-Auriga star-forming region, comprising 69 class III and 5 class I/II YSOs with spectral types B9-M3, as part of a total sample of 149 class II and 82 class III YSOs. This represents a complete sample (100%) of class II and III YSOs with spectral types earlier than K3, and a near-complete sample (85%) for spectral types earlier than M2. The survey has a median $3\sigma$ sensitivity of 1.4mJy. We did not find any emission from circumstellar dust around class III YSOs, but present three detections that can be attributed to variable stellar activity, and one from an unresolved companion. We compile and model spectral energy distributions (SEDs) for the sample, and report 27 class III YSOs with excess thermal emission. We demonstrate that the class III YSOs in Taurus are typically older than their class II counterparts. We produce millimeter luminosity and dust disk mass distributions, and present evidence for a bifurcation between the class II and III populations, implying that ${\gtrsim}99.5\%$ of the dust mass is dispersed or transformed as YSOs transition from the class II to III stage. The combined infrared and millimeter properties demonstrate that warm (inner) and cold (outer) dust reservoirs evolve on comparable timescales: there is a rapid evolution across the radial extent of disks. We demonstrate that the survey properties are broadly consistent with a belt population that formed planetesimals from class II disks with an efficiency of a few tenths to a few tens of percent.

2611.22150.abstract: If we could observe the Solar System's giant planets with the upcoming Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), the dominant sources of reflected near-infrared light would not always be the planets themselves. In fact, the brightest sources are split roughly evenly between the giants and their icy companions: at the locations of the giant planets, the dominant point sources would be Jupiter, Saturn's rings, Uranus, and Triton (Neptune's icy moon). Motivated by these Solar System cases in which rings or moons outshine their host planets, we investigate the detectability of analogous exomoons and exorings with HWO. We compute the expected signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) for moons and rings with the same albedos as their Solar System counterparts over a range of sizes, system distances, and star to planet+moon or star to planet+ring separations. We find that reflected light from Triton-analog exomoons and Saturn-analog exorings is detectable with HWO over a broad parameter space. In the nearest systems, icy Titan-sized moons are detectable at star-moon separations of ~2 AU and icy Earth-sized moons out to ~6 AU. Moreover, Saturn-like exorings are likely to be the brightest point sources in many extrasolar systems, capable of greatly outshining any planets, while remaining potentially detectable at system distances out to 100 pc. These results highlight the need for further work to develop methods for identifying and disentangling exoring and exomoon signatures from exoplanet signals in HWO observations, where these sources will be blended and spatially unresolved.

2611.22225.abstract: FU Orionis (FUor) outbursts are high-accretion events in protoplanetary disks thought to be driven by the magnetorotational instability (MRI). Although these outbursts span a wide range of observed durations and can thermally process and potentially transport disk material, the physical processes governing their decay remain poorly understood. We present a three-dimensional radiative non-ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulation of the decay of an MRI-driven FUor outburst, complemented by a suite of two-dimensional models that explore its dependence on disk properties. During the decay, rings and gaps form naturally within the inner disk. Magnetic flux preferentially concentrates in the gaps, while the rings remain comparatively weakly magnetized. We show that MRI-active rings act as ``magnetic dams,'' confining magnetic flux within adjacent gaps. As the rings cool below the MRI activation temperature, non-ideal MHD effects decouple the gas from the magnetic field, allowing the trapped flux to diffuse outward. This outward diffusion can sometimes transiently reactivate MRI in neighboring rings, producing localized reheating events that we term ``Reactivation.'' By comparing otherwise identical two- and three-dimensional simulations, we find that MRI heating is systematically less efficient in two dimensions, leading to outburst durations shorter by a factor of $\sim3$--4. Our model suite further shows that the decay timescale depends primarily on the disk surface density and distance from the central star, with only a weak dependence on the magnetic field strength. We further derive an empirical relation linking the outburst duration to these quantities.

2611.22571.title: Planet Formation in a Warped Disc: Gravitational Instability and Misaligned Infall

figures.caption: Figure 1: The simulation setup after the infalling material has been initialised. The disc has already been evolved for 4 outer orbits until gravitational instabilities developed. The infall is initialised as an elliptical cloud of gas that is one-third of the disc mass. The disc and cloud are initially misaligned by $135^{\circ}$ as shown by the unit angular momentum vectors in the bottom right.

Figure 2: The evolution of the surface density of a $0.15M_{\odot}$ disc as it interacts with a $0.05M_{\odot}$ cloud of infalling gas. The top and bottom panels show the face-on and edge-on views, respectively. From left to right, the panels show the disc at 5 orbits before infall has impacted the disc, at 6.33 orbits as the disc begins to interact with the infalling gas, and at 7.65 orbits after a period of continuous infall onto the disc. Before infall, the spiral arms driven by gravitational instability are symmetric, and the disc is coplanar. As infall initially impacts the disc, the spiral structures weaken and become more asymmetric. The misaligned infall also begins to warp the disc. After a period of continuous infall, the spiral arms return to being symmetric as gravitational instability once again becomes the dominant process as the disc mass gradually increases. The warp also becomes stronger, evident in the edge-on view where the spiral arms are misaligned relative to the inner disc. Eventually, one of the spiral arms becomes gravitationally unstable and fragments to form a planet, as shown in the zoomed-in insets.

Figure 3: Radial profiles of the disc tilt (top panel), twist (middle panel), and warp amplitude (bottom panel) at 7.65 orbits. The solid circle marks the location of the fragment. The disc is strongly twisted with minor misalignments as seen by the low tilt values, but a radially dependent twist which is consistent with differential precession. The smooth increase in the warp amplitude shows that the disc remains continuous, with the strength of the warp increasing towards the outer regions of the disc.

Figure 4: The top panels show the surface density of the disc at 5 (left panel) and 7.65 orbits (right panel), before and after the disc has been perturbed by infall, respectively. The extracted location of each spiral is plotted on top of the image. The bottom panels show the pitch angles of each spiral arm calculated using Eq. 6. The pitch angles before infall are constant with radius, consistent with past studies of isolated gravitationally unstable discs. However, after infall the pitch angles increase with radius.

Figure 5: The evolution of the spiral arms at a fixed radius of $R=77$ au as a function of azimuthal angle $phi$, and time. Before infall (at $t<6$ orbits), the spiral arms are straight diagonal lines, indicating a constant pattern speed at a specific radius, consistent with expectations of isolated gravitationally unstable discs. After infall, the pattern speed increases as evident by the steeper gradient. Additionally, there is a slight bend which moves towards smaller $\phi$ over time as the effects of infall extends to the entire disc.

Figure 6: Azimuthally averaged profiles of the surface density (top panel), temperature (middle panel), and Toomre $$Q$$ (bottom panel) at 5, 6.33, and 7.65 orbits. The infalling gas causes mass to be redistributed from the outer disc towards the inner disc. Additionally, the disc temperatures increase due to envelope backwarming. Although Toomre Q indicates that the disc should become gravitationally stable as a result, this is a limitation of azimuthally averaging.

Figure 7: All three lines show the azimuthally averaged temperature at 7.65 orbits. The black line uses all particles in the simulations and includes $P\mathrm{d}V$ work and shock heating. The blue line shows the temperature recalculated by mcfost after excluding the cloud particles. The orange line shows the temperatures obtained without including $P\mathrm{d}V$ work and shock heating. There are minor differences in the temperatures without $P\mathrm{d}V$ work and shock heating. However, the disc is cooler when the cloud particles are removed. Thus, radiative interactions with the surrounding infalling gas is the dominant reason for the disc becoming warmer.

Figure 8: Two-dimensional plots of Toomre $$$$Q$$$$ at 5, 6.33, and 7.65 orbits. The grey dashed line marks ${Q=1.4}$. At 5 orbits, pre-infall, the low Q regions in red correspond to the spiral arms as expected. At 6.33 orbits, most of the disc has ${${Q>1.4}$}$, consistent with the azimuthally averaged profile in Fig 6. However, at the location where infall first impacts the disc (top right quadrant), there is a region of low Q, highlighting the localised nature of infall. At 7.33 orbits, the spiral arms once again correspond to low Q. However, they are messier due to the continued effect of infall. Thus, gravitational instabilities are still visible due to local conditions even when the azimuthally averaged criterion, Q>1.4 is not satisfied.

Figure 9: Synthetic images of the disc at $1.6\,\mu$m when viewed edge-on at 5 and 7.65 orbits. Since the disc is coplanar before infall (top panel), the flux from the upper disc surfaces is symmetric. After infall (bottom panel), there is a lateral asymmetry in the flux due to the disc being warped.

Figure 10: Synthetic images of the disc at $1.3\mathrm{\,mm}$ at 5 and 7.65 orbits when viewed face-on and edge-on are shown in the top and bottom panels, respectively. Infalling gas increases the disc mass and decreases the radial extent of the disc. Thus, the contrast of the spiral arms is lower due to the increased optical depth of the disc. The warp induced by infall is also evident in the edge-on view where the misaligned spiral arms result in vertical asymmetries. The infalling gas itself is also visible in both the face-on and edge-on view.

2611.22571.abstract: We perform three-dimensional smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations to investigate the impact of misaligned infall on a gravitationally unstable protoplanetary disc. The interaction between the disc and the infalling gas does not occur uniformly across all radii. As infall impacts the outer disc first, the outer disc experiences stronger torques than the inner disc, resulting in a warped disc where the angular momentum vector of the disc varies with radius. The surrounding infalling gas reprocesses stellar irradiation and re-emits it back towards the disc, resulting in a warmer disc. The higher temperatures cause the disc to become more gravitationally stable resulting in weaker spiral arms. However, over time, infall also continuously increases the disc mass, gradually altering the local conditions and strengthening gravitational instabilities despite the azimuthally averaged Toomre $Q$ indicating that the disc is stable against gravitational instability. Eventually, one of the spiral arms fragments, forming a giant planet by gravitational instability in a disc warped by misaligned infall. Hence, the impact of infall on gravitational instability in general will vary depending on the infall and disc properties due to the balance between the stabilising and destabilising effects. We also find that infall alters the expected signatures of gravitationally unstable discs by introducing asymmetries in scattered-light, continuum, and molecular line emission.

2611.22913.abstract: We present the Grain Residence-Time Method (GRTM), a computationally efficient particle-tracking approach for studying dust evolution and trapping in protoplanetary disks. By reconstructing steady-state dust distributions from particle residence times, this method provides a way to obtain radial dust surface density profiles without directly evolving the dust as a fluid. We compare the GRTM with dust profiles computed via standard methods using the $\texttt{FARGO3D}$ code, which models the dust as a pressureless fluid, and find very good agreement over a wide range of parameter space. Finally, we investigate how dust gap formation depends on the planet-to-star mass ratio ($q$) and Stokes number ($\mathrm{St}$), through a parameter study, establishing an empirical criterion for dust gap opening. In doing so, we have discovered a new regime of gap opening for small grains with $St \lesssim 10^{-2}$ and for planet mass well below Jupiter's, which is likely very relevant for gaps seen in ALMA images.

2611.22952.abstract: External photoevaporation is increasingly recognised as an important influence on protoplanetary disk evolution. However, there are no established molecular line diagnostics that can reliably distinguish external irradiation from variations in intrinsic stellar and disk properties. We use a large grid of thermochemical models to predict the fluxes of 48 transitions from eight species observable with ALMA, spanning a wide range of system properties and external FUV fields of 100 to 100,000 G0. At fixed stellar and disk properties, all transitions generally brighten with increasing FUV field strength. HCO+ and CO fluxes increase monotonically in virtually all disks, whereas lower-excitation lines, particularly those of C2H and N2H+, respond weakly and non-monotonically. However, variations in stellar mass and disk size introduce substantial degeneracies, limiting the usefulness of individual line fluxes as tracers of external irradiation. We therefore assess all pairwise line flux ratios, which can significantly reduce these degeneracies, evaluating their correlation with the external field, the magnitude of their change across the FUV range, and predicted ALMA detectability. We identify 135 promising ratios, including several combining strong FUV sensitivity and high detectability with efficient single-tuning ALMA observations. The strongest diagnostics either contrast high- and low-excitation lines of the same or co-spatial species (e.g. CO J=8-7/J=1-0), probing different regions of the photoevaporative wind, or pair an FUV-sensitive wind tracer with comparatively insensitive emission arising closer to the disk (e.g. HCO+ J=3-2/C2H N=3-2). Our results provide a framework for identifying externally photoevaporating systems from spatially unresolved emission and constraining their incident FUV field strengths.

2611.23217.abstract: Compact multi-planet systems exhibit a tendency for planetary radii to follow ordered sequences with orbital position, suggesting that these non-random patterns preserve a fossil record of their formation. Here, we investigate whether ordering of planet radii and masses with orbital period is related to proximity to mean-motion resonances. We compare near-resonant and non-resonant systems using complementary rank- and inversion-based measures of ordering, while accounting for differences in planet multiplicity and uncertainties in the measured planetary properties. We find that radii and masses are less monotonically ordered in near-resonant systems than in non-resonant systems, with the primary radius analysis providing stronger evidence than the mass analysis. This result is opposite to the naive expectation that dynamical instabilities should erase the primordial ordering of initially resonant systems and leave non-resonant systems in a more disordered state.

2611.21786.abstract: We present a multi-wavelength case study of the star T28 in the Chamaeleon I star-forming region and investigate the dust evolution of its highly Ca-depleted protoplanetary disk. We combine new observations from the MIKE spectrograph on the Magellan Clay Telescope with archival IRS spectrum and photometry. We constrain the optical extinction using the hydrogen column density of the region, and apply ROTFIT to obtain stellar parameters. We estimate the mass accretion rate by fitting the excess flux above the photosphere with an accretion shock model. We model the line profiles of Ca II K and H$\alpha$ with magnetospheric accretion models to infer Ca/H abundance, while the infrared excess is modeled with irradiated accretion disk models to get disk properties. We find that T28 is a high accretor with significant Ca depletion in its accretion flows. We find that the disk is best fit with a pre-transitional model with a disk mass of 0.12 $M_{\odot}$, where two optically thick disks are separated by a gap filled with optically thin dust extending to 16 au. This gap would not be resolved in the existing observations. T28 follows the trend of increasing depletion with increasing mass accretion rate. This trend can potentially be explained by preferential and early giant planet formation in massive disks, as suggested by recent planet formation simulations, leading to enhanced capture of refractory material in the massive disks of high accretors and thus depletion in the material reaching the star.

2611.21800.abstract: Brown dwarfs occupy the mass range between stars and planets, populations whose dominant formation channels differ, which leave measurable differences in the orbital eccentricity and host-star metallicity distributions. We assemble a sample of astrometric binaries with main sequence primaries and brown dwarf companions at $\mathcal{O}$(AU) separations from $\textit{Gaia}$ DR3. The observable photocenter motions for such binaries are degenerate between a genuinely low-mass companion and a near-equal-mass binary. We break this degeneracy using $\textit{Gaia}$ XP spectrophotometry and follow-up FEROS spectroscopy, which removes removes ${\sim}70\%$ of initial low-mass-function candidates as likely near-twin binaries and leaves residual contamination of only a few percent. The resulting 368 systems, with masses and metallicities determined from the XP spectra and a selection function forward-modelled with $\texttt{Gaiamock}$, form the largest homogeneous sample of brown dwarf companions with astrometric orbits. We find the eccentricity distribution to be well described by a normal distribution. This is comparable to eccentricities of stellar companions at the same periods and higher than those of giant planets, with no significant dependence on companion mass ($\alpha=-0.13\pm0.09$) or period ($\beta=0.10\pm0.05$). The host-star metallicity distribution is likewise stellar-like, extending to [M/H]$=-0.5$, in contrast to the predominantly super-solar metallicity hosts of giant planets. After accounting for selection, the companion-mass distribution over all brown dwarf masses is consistent with an extension of stellar-binary demographics. Brown dwarf companions at AU separations down to at least $20\,M_J$ therefore appear to form predominantly through a binary-star-like channel. A possible transition to planet-like formation at lower masses cannot be located with the present sample.

2611.22800.abstract: Ancient Chinese records of lunar occultations of planets have been used to test planetary theories and investigate long-term changes in Earth's rotation. However, certain records contain identification errors whose origins remain poorly understood; we propose that some of these errors may arise from misidentifying guest stars, such as novae or supernovae, as planets. We analyzed 67 errata on lunar occultations of planets from Liu Ci-Yuan's (2015) monograph using modern ephemerides and the open-source Python package \texttt{occultsky}, publicly available on GitHub. Using recorded dates and dynastic capital coordinates, we constructed observing windows anchored at solar noon and extending by $\pm 1$ day. Each window covered the preceding and recorded nights because the date may be off by one day. For each of the 67 records, we cataloged the apparent right ascension and declination $(\alpha, \delta)$ at the midpoint of the Moon's visibility window on each candidate night. The band swept by the lunar disk confines a possible transient to a narrow region a few degrees across; these midpoint coordinates serve as proxies for the implied guest-star positions. The catalog supplies candidate positions rather than identifications, enabling remnant and compact-object searches to test the guest-star hypothesis directly. If associations are established, these records could become dated guest-star candidates, and their dates could anchor remnant ages.
